title: Optional return silently causes AttributeError at runtime

hints.title: Where to look
hints.body: Open `src/user_service.py` and find the `get_user_email` function. Notice that `users.get(user_id)` returns `Optional[User]` — it can return `None` if the key is absent. But the very next line does `user.email` without any check. If `user_id` is not in the dict, this raises `AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'email'` at runtime.

hints.title: The concept
hints.body: This is a **missing None check** (also called a null-safety bug). Python's `dict.get()` returns `Optional[T]` — the type hint tells you it can be `None`. The function signature says it returns `str`, which mypy enforces. When mypy runs in `--strict` mode it will flag `user.email` as an error because `user` is `Optional[User]`, not `User`. The fix is to explicitly handle the `None` case **before** accessing the attribute — either with `if user is None: raise ...` or with an `assert user is not None`.

hints.title: The fix approach
hints.body:
Add an explicit guard immediately after the `.get()` call:
```python
def get_user_email(user_id: str) -> str:
    user = users.get(user_id)   # Optional[User]
    if user is None:
        raise KeyError(f"User '{user_id}' not found")
    return user.email            # Safe: mypy knows user is User here
```
This makes the intent explicit, gives callers a clear `KeyError` with a useful message instead of a confusing `AttributeError: 'NoneType'`, and satisfies mypy strict mode. Alternatively, you could raise `ValueError`, or use `assert user is not None, ...` — any pattern that guards the `None` case before the attribute access.

badPatches.title: bare except: pass swallows the error without fixing the root cause
